title: Chapter 10: Algorithms, Recursion, and Complexity
description: Build transferable problem-solving skill through invariants and measured complexity. Learners implement and test linear and binary search, compare sorting strategies, trace recursive and backtracking call trees, apply two-pointer, window, frequency-map, BFS, and DFS patterns, and optimize only after proving the direct solution and locating its actual bottleneck.

lessons.title: Big-O, best/average/worst case, and practical costs

exercises.title: Big-O, best/average/worst case, and practical costs: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Two nested loops visit every distinct pair. What is their growth?
hints: Recall that nested loops visiting every distinct pair perform on the order of n(n-1)/2 comparisons, which grows quadratically as n increases.

lessons.title: Linear search, binary search, and insertion points

exercises.title: Linear search, binary search, and insertion points: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: What can lowerBound return when every element is below target?
hints: Recall that lowerBound's half-open interval [low, high) shrinks to low == high == length when every element is below target, since that is the correct insertion point past the end.

lessons.title: Sorting algorithms, stability, and comparator correctness

exercises.title: Sorting algorithms, stability, and comparator correctness: concept check
choices: Original relative order of equal-key elements
hints: Recall that insertion sort's strict-greater-than comparison (values[j] > current) never swaps two equal elements past each other, which is what keeps their original relative order.

lessons.title: Recursion, call stacks, divide-and-conquer, and backtracking

exercises.title: Recursion, call stacks, divide-and-conquer, and backtracking: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Why must a backtracking algorithm restore its working list?
choices: Sibling branches must start from the correct prior state
Every branch should share all prior choices
hints: Recall that backtracking reuses one mutable working list across branches; undoing the last choice after exploring it is what lets a sibling branch start from the correct prior state instead of an accumulated one.

lessons.title: Two pointers, sliding windows, maps, BFS, and DFS

exercises.title: Two pointers, sliding windows, maps, BFS, and DFS: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: When does BFS give shortest paths by edge count?
choices: For arbitrary weighted edges without modification
Only for graphs with no cycles
hints: Recall that BFS expands the frontier one edge at a time, so the first time it reaches a node is guaranteed shortest only when every edge counts the same, i.e. the graph is unweighted.

exercises.title: Algorithms, Recursion, and Complexity: professional judgment
exercises.instructionMarkdown: An optimization changes O(n squared) to O(n) but uses more memory. What should be documented?
choices: Input assumptions and the time-space tradeoff

exercises.title: Chapter 10 implementation lab: lowerBound
exercises.instructionMarkdown:
Implement `lowerBound`. In a sorted array return the first index whose value is at least target, or length when none exists. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

Input is sorted ascending, non-null, and may contain duplicates.
hints: Find the first index whose value is at least target (>=), not the first index strictly greater than target.
Trace the public example plus a boundary where target exceeds every element and one where duplicates surround the target value.

exercises.title: Lower-bound duplicate handling
exercises.instructionMarkdown: The loop advances `lo` whenever `a[mid] <= 3`, which computes the index past the last matching duplicate (an upper bound) instead of the first index at least 3, so it prints `3` instead of `1` on `{1,3,3,8}`. Repair the comparison so the search narrows toward the first value at least target, keeping the demonstrated array and target, and explain why the corrected comparison lands on the earlier index; do not replace it with a hard-coded print. Output tests verify the result; preserving the intended operation requires source review.
hints: The required index is the first value at least 3, not the first value above 3.

exercises.title: Priority issue index
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Implement IssueIndex.run(String input). Each nonblank line is id|priority|title. Trim tokens. id is a positive int, priority is 1..3, title is nonempty and contains no pipe. Reject malformed lines and repeated IDs (keep the first accepted record); each rejection increments ERRORS. Sort accepted records by descending priority then ascending id. Output id|priority|title lines followed by ERRORS=<count>. Empty input returns ERRORS=0. Distinct tasks with the same priority must all survive. Return \n-separated text without trailing newline. Use a record for a task and a collection with an explicit uniqueness policy.
hints: Parse and validate all fields before mutating state. Split with a negative limit when empty fields must be preserved.
Choose collections according to identity and ordering requirements. Build output lines and join them with a newline.
